A **glioma** is a type of [tumor](Neoplasm "Neoplasm") that starts in the [glial cells](Glial_cells "Glial cells") of the [brain](Human_brain "Human brain") or the [spine](Vertebral_column "Vertebral column").[[1]](Glioma#cite_note-1) Gliomas comprise about 30 percent of all [brain tumors](Brain_tumor "Brain tumor") and central nervous system tumours, and 80 percent of all malignant brain tumours.[[2]](Glioma#cite_note-Goodenberger2012-2)

## Signs and symptoms

Symptoms of gliomas depend on which part of the central nervous system is affected. A brain glioma can cause [headaches](Headaches "Headaches"), [vomiting](Nausea "Nausea"), [seizures](Seizures "Seizures"), and [cranial nerve](Cranial_nerve "Cranial nerve") disorders as a result of increased intracranial pressure. A glioma of the [optic nerve](Optic_nerve "Optic nerve") can cause vision loss. Spinal cord gliomas can cause [pain](Pain "Pain"), [weakness](Weakness "Weakness"), or [numbness](Numbness "Numbness") in the extremities. Gliomas do not usually [metastasize](Metastasis "Metastasis") by the bloodstream, but they can spread via the [cerebrospinal fluid](Cerebrospinal_fluid "Cerebrospinal fluid") and cause "drop metastases" to the spinal cord. Complex visual hallucinations have been described as a symptom of low-grade glioma.[[3]](Glioma#cite_note-3)

A child who has a subacute disorder of the central nervous system that produces cranial nerve abnormalities (especially of cranial nerve VII and the lower bulbar nerves), long-tract signs, unsteady gait secondary to spasticity, and some behavioral changes is most likely to have a pontine glioma.[[4]](Glioma#cite_note-4)

## Causes

### Hereditary disorders

The exact causes of gliomas are not known. [Hereditary disorders](Genetic_disorders "Genetic disorders") such as [neurofibromatoses](Neurofibromatoses "Neurofibromatoses") (type 1 and type 2) and [tuberous sclerosis complex](Tuberous_sclerosis_complex "Tuberous sclerosis complex") are known to predispose to their development.[[5]](Glioma#cite_note-5) Different oncogenes can cooperate in the development of gliomas.[[6]](Glioma#cite_note-6)

### Diet

Some studies of diet and vitamin supplementation appear to point out that dietary <N-nitroso> compounds may affect the risk of both childhood and adult brain tumors. Researchers have observed in some studies that brain tumor patients (or their mothers) have generally consumed more cured foods (also known as [Curing](Curing_(food_preservation) "Curing (food preservation)")) than control groups. **Oligodendrogliomas** are a type of [glioma](Glioma "Glioma") that are believed to originate from the [oligodendrocytes](Oligodendrocyte "Oligodendrocyte") of the [brain](Brain "Brain") or from a glial precursor cell. They occur primarily in adults (9.4% of all primary brain and central nervous system tumors) but are also found in children (4% of all primary brain tumors).

## Signs and symptoms

Oligodendroglioma arise mainly in the [frontal lobe](Frontal_lobe "Frontal lobe") and in 50–80% of cases, the first symptom is the onset of [seizure](Seizure "Seizure") activity, without having any symptoms beforehand.[[2]](Oligodendroglioma#cite_note-Oligodendroglioma-2) <Headaches> combined with increased [intracranial pressure](Intracranial_pressure "Intracranial pressure") are also a common symptom of oligodendroglioma. Depending on the location of the tumor, many different neurological and neuropsychological deficits can be induced, including, but not limited to, visual loss, motor weakness, cognitive decline, and [anxiety](Anxiety "Anxiety").[[3]](Oligodendroglioma#cite_note-3) A [computed tomography](Computed_tomography "Computed tomography") (CT) or [magnetic resonance imaging](Magnetic_resonance_imaging "Magnetic resonance imaging") (MRI) scan is necessary to characterize tumor size, location, and hetero- or homogeneity. Final diagnosis relies on [biopsy](Biopsy "Biopsy") and [histopathologic](Histopathologic "Histopathologic") examination of the tumor mass.[[2]](Oligodendroglioma#cite_note-Oligodendroglioma-2)

## Cause

The cause of oligodendrogliomas is unknown. Some studies have linked oligodendroglioma with a viral cause. A 2009 Oxford Neurosymposium study illustrated a 69% correlation between NJDS gene mutation and the tumor initiation. A single case report has linked oligodendroglioma to irradiation of pituitary adenoma.[[4]](Oligodendroglioma#cite_note-4)[[5]](Oligodendroglioma#cite_note-5)

Historically, medulloblastomas have been classified as a [primitive neuroectodermal tumor](Primitive_neuroectodermal_tumor "Primitive neuroectodermal tumor") (PNET), but it is now known that medulloblastoma is distinct from supratentorial PNETs and they are no longer considered similar entities.[[4]](Medulloblastoma#cite_note-4) Medulloblastomas are invasive, rapidly growing tumors that, unlike most brain tumors, spread through the [cerebrospinal fluid](Cerebrospinal_fluid "Cerebrospinal fluid") and frequently [metastasize](Metastasis "Metastasis") to different locations along the surface of the brain and spinal cord. Metastasis all the way down to the [cauda equina](Cauda_equina "Cauda equina") at the base of the spinal cord is termed "drop metastasis". [Positional vertigo](Positional_vertigo "Positional vertigo") and [nystagmus](Pathologic_nystagmus "Pathologic nystagmus") are also frequent, and facial sensory loss or motor weakness may be present. attacks appear late in the disease. **Meningioma**, also known as **meningeal tumor**, is typically a slow-growing tumor that forms from the [meninges](Meninges "Meninges"), the membranous layers surrounding the [brain and spinal cord](Central_nervous_system "Central nervous system").[[1]](Meningioma#cite_note-NCI2016-1) Symptoms depend on the location and occur as a result of the tumor pressing on nearby tissue.[[3]](Meningioma#cite_note-Wi2010-3)[[6]](Meningioma#cite_note-WCR2014-6) Many cases never produce symptoms.[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2) Occasionally [seizures](Seizures "Seizures"), [dementia](Dementia "Dementia"), trouble talking, vision problems, one sided weakness, or [loss of bladder control](Urinary_incontinence "Urinary incontinence") may occur.[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2)

Risk factors include exposure to [ionizing radiation](Ionizing_radiation "Ionizing radiation") such as during [radiation therapy](Radiation_therapy "Radiation therapy"), a family history of the condition, and [neurofibromatosis type 2](Neurofibromatosis_type_2 "Neurofibromatosis type 2").[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2)[[3]](Meningioma#cite_note-Wi2010-3) They appear to be able to form from a number of different types of [cells](Cell_(biology) "Cell (biology)") including [arachnoid](Arachnoid_mater "Arachnoid mater") cells.[[1]](Meningioma#cite_note-NCI2016-1)[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2) Diagnosis is typically by [medical imaging](Medical_imaging "Medical imaging").[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2)

If there are no symptoms, periodic observation may be all that is required.[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2) Most cases that result in symptoms can be cured by surgery.[[1]](Meningioma#cite_note-NCI2016-1) Following complete removal fewer than 20% recur.[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2) If surgery is not possible or all the tumor cannot be removed, [radiosurgery](Radiosurgery "Radiosurgery") may be helpful.[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2) <Chemotherapy> has not been found to be useful.[[2]](Meningioma#cite_note-Fer2018-2) A small percentage grow rapidly and are associated with worse outcomes.[[1]](Meningioma#cite_note-NCI

content:
Based on my research of medical literature, here are 4 primary brain tumors and a genetic mutation associated with each one:

## 1. **Glioblastoma (GBM)** - **IDH1/IDH2 mutations**
Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults. Mutations in the *IDH1* (isocitrate dehydrogenase 1) and *IDH2* genes occur in approximately 80% of low-grade gliomas and secondary high-grade gliomas. These mutations lead to production of the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which alters DNA and histone methylation patterns. GBM is also associated with mutations in *EGFR*, *PTEN*, and *TP53*.

## 2. **Oligodendroglioma** - **1p/19q co-deletion**
Oligodendrogliomas are gliomas that arise from oligodendrocytes. They are characterized by a chromosomal alteration known as combined deletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q (co-deletion), which is found in 50-80% of cases. These tumors also typically harbor *IDH1* or *IDH2* mutations. The combination of 1p/19q co-deletion and IDH mutations helps distinguish oligodendrogliomas from other glioma types.

## 3. **Medulloblastoma** - **PTCH1 mutations**
Medulloblastoma is a common primary brain cancer in children that originates in the cerebellum. Mutations in the *PTCH1* (Patched-1) gene, which is part of the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway, are associated with the SHH-subgroup of medulloblastomas. Other mutations seen in medulloblastoma include *TP53*, *SUFU*, and *MYC* family gene amplifications.

## 4. **Meningioma** - **NF2 mutations**
Meningiomas are typically slow-growing tumors that arise from the meninges (membranous layers surrounding the brain). Mutations in the *NF2* gene (neurofibromin 2), also known as the merlin gene, are found in approximately 50% of sporadic meningiomas and nearly all meningiomas in patients with neurofibromatosis type 2. The *NF2* gene is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 22.
